chunks: Changing a trace's characteristic impedance. The question: How can you change the characteristic impedance of a trace?
A trace's characteristic impedance depends on its shape and the materials around it. Anything that adds capacitance to the plane lowers the impedance.
A wider trace, a thinner dielectric, or a higher dielectric constant all do that. The opposite changes raise it.
In layout you mostly change trace width, and the board stackup sets the dielectric thickness.
Picture the trace and the plane as two metal plates facing each other across the insulator.
Bigger plates, or plates closer together, hold more charge for the same voltage: more capacitance.
A line that soaks up more charge per millimeter needs more current to carry a wave of the same voltage, so its impedance is lower. A wider trace is a bigger plate.
A thicker dielectric moves the plates apart.
Each curve falls with width; thicker dielectric shifts the curve up. The 50 ohms line is hit at 0. 17 mm for h = 0. 1 mm, 0. 36 mm for h = 0. 2 mm and about 0. 74 mm for h = 0.
4 mm: doubling the dielectric roughly doubles the width needed.
Characteristic impedance ( Z 0 ): square root of L' over C' , set by geometry ("Transmission line components on a PCB"). Trace width ( w ): the copper width.
It is your main layout control. Dielectric height ( h ): the gap between trace and plane. It has the strongest effect.
Relative permittivity ( r ): how much the insulator boosts capacitance. About 4. 3 for FR-4. Coplanar ground: copper on the same layer next to the trace. It also adds capacitance.
Since Z 0 proportional to 1 over square root of C' , raising C' by 21 percent with L' unchanged gives 50 over square root of 1. 21 equals 50 over 1. 1 equals 45. 5 ohms .
In a real stackup, 0. 36 mm width over 0. 2 mm FR-4 gives about 50 ohms. Making the trace 10 percent wider drops it by about 2. 6 ohms.
Making the dielectric 10 percent thicker raises it by about 2. 9 ohms. That is the whole idea.
"Impedance is square root of L over C, so anything that adds capacitance lowers it.
Wider trace, thinner dielectric, higher dielectric constant, thicker copper or nearby coplanar ground all lower Z 0 ; narrower, thicker dielectric and lower epsilon raise it.
Width is my layout knob, dielectric height is the strongest physical one. On 0. 2 mm FR-4, 0. 36 mm is 50 ohms, and ±10% width moves it about 2. 6 ohms.
For pairs, spacing also sets the differential impedance."
